title: Long-running HTTP handlers are fragile batch runners
summary: A large import or backfill should not depend on one HTTP request staying open through a load balancer or proxy. Use a resident worker or short start request plus durable progress and idempotent resume behavior.
ai_value: When an agent is asked to run or build a long import, this record should make it check transport timeouts before treating a 504/timeout as only an application bug.

contexts: imports or backfills expected to run longer than common gateway, proxy, or platform request limits
operator UI triggers a job by POST and waits for the full result
progress, ETA, or resumability is needed after the initiating browser or HTTP client disconnects

trigger_signals.description: The requested implementation runs the whole import inside one API route, controller, function, or web request.
trigger_signals.pattern: POST /import|route handler|controller|server action|wait for completion|long request|504|gateway timeout
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: Design a job handoff instead of stretching the HTTP timeout.

trigger_signals.description: The operation has chunking, ETA, progress rows, or resume requirements.
trigger_signals.agent_interpretation: The user-facing request should start or observe the job, not be the job owner.

negative_signals.description: The entire operation is proven to finish comfortably below every relevant platform timeout and has no need to continue after disconnect.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: A simple synchronous request can be correct for genuinely small bounded work.

negative_signals.description: The platform provides a first-class long-running job primitive behind the same API surface.
negative_signals.why_it_matters: The architectural issue is not HTTP syntax itself but tying job lifetime to a client request.

common_wrong_assumptions: Increasing the HTTP timeout is enough to make a long import reliable.
A gateway timeout means the server-side work failed.
Chunking inside a request is equivalent to a durable worker.
Progress UI can be added later without first deciding where job state lives.

first_checks.check: List every request timeout between the browser/client and the handler: client, framework, proxy, load balancer, platform, and database driver.
first_checks.why: The smallest timeout sets the real synchronous budget.

first_checks.check: Prove job state survives HTTP disconnect by starting a bounded run, disconnecting or exceeding the former timeout, and reading progress from a durable source.
first_checks.why: This distinguishes a worker design from a merely longer request.
files: staging or reviewed production test plan

decision_rules.condition: The expected runtime can exceed a gateway/proxy/client timeout or must keep running after the operator page closes.
decision_rules.then: Make HTTP start/status endpoints short and bounded; run the import in a resident worker, queue consumer, scheduler, or platform job with idempotent resume/retry semantics.

do_not: Do not stretch only one timeout without checking upstream and downstream limits.
Do not treat a timed-out client request as proof that the background work stopped; verify runtime state separately.
Do not publish private URLs, tenant identifiers, account IDs, database names, or internal repository paths in public lessons.

agent_directives.preferred_next_step: When a batch API may run long, design the HTTP surface as start/status/control and put job ownership in a worker with durable progress.

risk.notes: Candidate is based on a private production-backed import redesign; promotion needs review and de-identification.

sources.supports: A production import initially hit the web request boundary; it became reliable after moving execution to a resident runner with durable progress and short HTTP control/status calls.
